content.text: Chapter Thirteen
Silence from Beyond
By the third month, the Blood Knights had learned how little victory changed the Ghostlands.

Tranquillien still stood empty beneath a bruised evening sky. Rot stained its plaster walls. The inn roof had fallen inward, and pale weeds crowded the road where merchants had once argued over wagon space. No banner flew above the town. No cooking smoke rose from its chimneys. Scourge tracks crossed Amani prints in the mud, old violence overwritten by newer passage.

Falanaras withdrew north through the ruins with six Blood Knights, nine Farstriders, and three wounded scouts between them. They had entered before dawn to destroy a necromantic focus feeding the Dead Scar. The focus was broken. The creatures it had stirred were still coming.
“Left lane,” Lethira called from a roofless doorway. “Ghouls in the tannery yard. At least twelve.”

Theron shifted toward the opening before Falanaras answered. His shield file had become four knights instead of five after Althene remained at the boundary with the worst of the wounded. Four were enough. Red-gold radiance joined their shields in overlapping curves while the Farstriders carried the scouts past.

The ghouls struck the ward in a wave of claws and spoiled flesh. Theron gave half a step, caught the force across his legs, and held. The three knights beside him matched his draw without being told. M’uru’s pain entered the street as a thin vibration beneath the clash.

Months earlier, someone would have flared too brightly. Someone would have spent enough Light to burn the first rank apart and left the whole file weakened for the second. Now the barrier bent, endured, and gave Falanaras room to work.

He and Daric passed through the shields at opposite ends. Falanaras’s sword caught fire from hilt to point. He cut the nearest ghoul through the neck, turned under another creature’s reach, and drove the blade backward into its ribs. Daric’s heavy weapon rose and fell beside him with punishing economy. Each blow carried enough Light to ruin the bindings inside dead flesh. None wasted radiance on the air.
An arrow with black fletching struck the tannery lintel.
“Down,” Lethira said.

The living elves dropped. A volley hissed over them from the southern roofs. Black arrows entered skulls, joints, and open mouths. Serenya’s scouts never showed themselves. They had agreed on signals at the runestone boundary, then separated before entering the blight. Trust had advanced far enough to coordinate fields of fire. It had not advanced far enough for either patrol to sleep near the other.

Falanaras rose into the sudden gap and finished the last ghoul. The Light withdrew at his command. Hunger did not return; the power drawn from M’uru had quieted that ache before the patrol began. Fatigue remained, honest and deep in his arms. The captive’s broken music lingered after every use.
Daric wiped his sword on a ghoul’s ragged tunic. “I preferred our first battle.”
“You were nearly dismembered by an abomination.”
“The weather was better.”
Theron released the joined ward. “Your standards have declined.”

“Service does that.” Daric looked toward the ruined southern street. Nothing moved there except carrion moths and one strip of black cloth tied to a gutter spike. Serenya’s signal meant the way remained open for another hundred paces. “We should continue degrading with purpose.”

They left Tranquillien before full dark. The town remained behind them for the Scourge, the Amani, and anything else willing to inhabit a place soaked in too many kinds of death. At the runestone boundary, wardens opened a narrow passage and counted every returning face. The Forsaken were already gone. A bundle of recovered dispatches waited beneath a black arrow at the edge of the road.

Limited coordination, the reports called it. The phrase concealed how often a gray hand had marked an ambush before living blood reached it, and how often red-gold Light had covered a dark ranger’s retreat. It also concealed the way Liadrin’s mouth hardened whenever those reports crossed her table.
The Blood Knights had proven their worth. Southern Eversong still needed proving every week.
Outland arrived in Silvermoon every fourth morning.

The schedule was never publicly posted, yet the Court of the Sun learned it. Families gathered near the sealed magisterial annex before dawn. Quartermasters came with tablets and carts. Petitioners carried letters for sons, daughters, spouses, and commanders serving beneath a sky they had never seen. Traders waited with requests for Netherstorm crystals and Zangarmarsh medicines. Children traded descriptions of Hellfire Peninsula as though the red wastes were a province awaiting proper roads.

The Portal stood far to the south in the Blasted Lands, held behind blood elf fortifications and watched from distant ridges by people who distrusted its keepers. Transit reports moved first through that garrison, then through a chain of secured relays. The final gate opened beneath Silvermoon only for approved cargo and personnel. Even so, the city had made a ritual of the arrivals.

Crimson ward-lines brightened across the annex doors. Magisters called names. Dusty soldiers emerged carrying sealed orders. Couriers surrendered metal cases into waiting hands. Sometimes a traveler halted beneath Silvermoon’s towers and wept before remembering that others could see.

Kael’thas rarely wrote to the city as a whole. He did not need to. His authority traveled in requisitions bearing the royal seal, casualty lists signed by his officers, and precise demands for metals, spell components, trained bodies, and patience. Each message assured Silvermoon that the prince still fought toward the future he had promised them.

Falanaras had crossed Outland and returned. The world remained more vivid in other people’s hopes than in his memory. They imagined a realm of power and opportunity. He remembered red dust in his teeth, naga counting every favor, soldiers burning over a Blade’s Edge gorge, and a luminous being lowering itself willingly into a cage.
Still, he watched each arrival.
On the morning Lord Sanguinar came home, the first warning was silence inside the annex.

The receiving spell faded. No magister called a name. Armored boots crossed the threshold with deliberate weight, and the waiting clerks moved aside before being ordered. Sanguinar emerged in scarlet plate darkened by Outland dust. Four soldiers followed him, all wearing the hard assurance of elves accustomed to command among strangers.

He had been broad-shouldered before Tempest Keep. Outland had pared him down without diminishing him. A pale scar ran from his left temple into his hair. His expression held the same fierce satisfaction Falanaras remembered from the assault staging grounds, when every casualty had seemed to confirm the worth of the objective.
Lady Liadrin waited at the foot of the annex stairs with Falanaras, Theron, and Daric behind her. Sanguinar bowed to the depth owed her rank and no farther.

“Lady Liadrin. Silvermoon has dressed your work well.” His gaze moved over the black armor and crimson tabards of the Blood Knights. “His Highness will be pleased to see it carried properly into his army.”
“The order serves Quel’Thalas,” Liadrin said. “You will learn its discipline before you carry its name anywhere.”
Sanguinar smiled. “Then teach me.”
M’uru’s chamber received the Outland delegation under triple guard.

The apparatus had changed since Falanaras’s binding. More conduits crossed the floor. Fresh wardstones stood in iron cradles along the walls, each part of another attempt to carry relief into the city above. Their inner light flickered weakly. The public system remained partial, unreliable, and hungry for magisterial attention. At the chamber’s center, individual binding still worked with brutal certainty.

M’uru hung within force-chains above the lowered dais. Its radiance filled the vault in slow pulses. The connection within Falanaras stirred in response, bringing warmth beneath his breastbone and the familiar note of suffering behind it.
Sanguinar looked up without awe. He studied the restraints, the conduits, and Astalor’s control table with a commander’s interest in a siege engine.

“Your bond will be personal, as every Blood Knight’s is,” Astalor said. “Our method has held across every distance we have tested, but passage between worlds remains unmeasured. After your return, you will report every interruption, surge, delay, or distortion. You will also remain within the measure we set. Mastery of the Light begins with command of one’s own appetite.”
“If the power answers, it will be used.”
“Your intention is clear,” Astalor said. “Our work requires observations, and you will provide them.”
Sanguinar’s smile returned. “You make conquest sound remarkably dull.”
Astalor adjusted one silver dial. “Properly governed, the bond is magnificent. Appetite is a poor substitute for mastery.”
Liadrin entered the binding circle with Sanguinar. “You will feel the source when the channel opens. Do not reach beyond the measure Astalor sets.”
“You doubt me.”
“I remember you.”

Astalor engaged the first restraint. Crimson bands tightened around M’uru. The chamber’s radiance drew inward, and the naaru’s cry passed through Falanaras before the sound reached his ears. Sanguinar’s shoulders locked. Gold flooded his fel-green eyes.
“Receive,” Liadrin ordered.

For a moment he obeyed. Red-gold Light gathered along his arms and settled beneath his skin. Then his right hand closed. The current lurched toward him. M’uru brightened in pain, and one of the force-chains rang against its pylon.
Liadrin struck him across the face.
The blow turned his head and broke his concentration. Astalor closed the channel. Light spilled from Sanguinar’s fingers in fading threads.
Sanguinar touched the corner of his mouth. Blood marked his thumb. “An old priest’s correction?”
“A commander’s. Reach again, and you leave without access to M’uru.”
His eyes remained bright with stolen gold. Anger passed through them, followed by calculation. He inclined his head.

The second attempt held. Sanguinar accepted the governed measure, settled into a sustained flow, and released it when ordered. M’uru’s radiance recovered to Astalor’s recorded baseline. The suffering within Falanaras did not recede as quickly.

One by one, the other Outland soldiers entered the circle. One wept without sound when the hunger vanished. Another vomited after hearing M’uru. A third failed twice before learning to let the current come without dragging at it. Liadrin dismissed the fourth when he lied about how much he had taken. Sanguinar watched them all with open impatience.
Afterward, Liadrin found Falanaras in the passage outside the chamber. Through the wall, the apparatus gave off a steady mechanical hum.

“At Tempest Keep,” she said, “Sanguinar ordered a wounded company back onto the bridge because their replacements had not arrived. The bridge was already lost. He knew it. He wanted the draenei to spend ammunition killing soldiers who could no longer hold a line.”
Falanaras remembered bodies beneath violet fire, too many uniforms fused into the crystal surface to know which officer had sent them. “Did it delay the defenders?”
“For less than a minute.” Liadrin looked toward the chamber doors. “He called the exchange favorable.”
“Why bind him?”

“Because the order cannot belong only to those I would choose as friends. Because Kael’thas commands an army beyond our reach, and that army is still ours.” Her voice hardened on the last word. “Because refusing him would keep the Light from soldiers who may need it while leaving Sanguinar exactly what he was.”
“And giving it to him?”
Liadrin’s gaze did not leave the doors. “May reveal what we have made.”
Sanguinar asked for a sparring partner the following afternoon.

Liadrin refused him twice. He pressed the request before the assembled order, framing it as a practical test of whether the new connection would withstand the return passage and whether Silvermoon’s doctrine could withstand Outland methods. Daric stepped forward before refusal became public humiliation.
“I have survived both,” Daric said. “One more comparison should be manageable.”

The practice court had been repaired since the order’s first weeks. New posts stood where uncontrolled flares had burned the old ones. Weapon racks lined the eastern wall. Fourteen Blood Knights formed a loose ring, joined by Sanguinar’s three successful companions and a pair of magisters assigned to measure each draw.
Daric carried a blunted greatsword. Sanguinar chose a single-handed war blade and no shield.
“First yield,” Liadrin said. “Bounded draw. No directed force above the breastplate.”
Sanguinar and Daric gave their word to the terms, then saluted.

They met in the center with enough force to send a hard report across the court. Daric used his greater reach to control the first exchange. Sanguinar slipped along the edge of each cut, testing wrists, knee, and shoulder with swift blows. He fought without Theron’s patience or Falanaras’s search for the power behind a line. He looked for pain and made it useful.

Daric caught him across the ribs. The blunted sword rang against plate hard enough to split skin beneath the cuirass. Sanguinar gave ground, smiling. He laid his free hand over the new wound, not to heal it, but to open a path from his pulse into the war blade. Heat climbed his veins. Crimson entered the red-gold radiance gathering along the steel, and the power took payment from him as it grew.
The blood-fed Light ignited around Sanguinar’s free hand and ran into his weapon.

Sanguinar used enough force to turn the exchange and no more than the terms permitted. Falanaras felt the draw as a sudden wrench beneath his breastbone. M’uru’s cry sharpened beneath the answering pain in Sanguinar’s ribs. He released the power through a low strike at Daric’s shield. Holy force burst across both weapons and drove Daric to one knee. Blood darkened the seam beneath Sanguinar’s cuirass. The advantage was real, costly, and legitimate.
“Keep it below the breastplate,” Liadrin warned.
Sanguinar reduced the flare. He circled while Daric stood. The obedience looked exact. Falanaras distrusted it more than open defiance.
Daric attacked again. Three heavy cuts drove Sanguinar toward the court wall. The third stopped at his throat.
“Yield,” Daric said.

Sanguinar seized the flat of Daric’s sword with his bare hand. The blood-fed radiance still stored in his weapon answered the motion, brightening as his own wound opened farther beneath the plate. He wrenched Daric’s blade aside and struck beneath the lifted arm.
The blow landed above the breastplate.

He released the stored force through Daric’s shoulder—above the pledged boundary. Radiance entered the joint with a flash bright enough to erase every shadow in the court. Bone cracked. Daric fell on his side, his sword skidding away. The contest had ended. Sanguinar kept the blood-fed current inside the broken shoulder anyway, spending his own pain to deepen another man’s after purpose was gone.
Falanaras crossed half the ring before thought caught him. His own sword was in his hand. Theron moved with him, shield raised.
Liadrin reached Sanguinar first. Her ranseur stopped against the hollow beneath his jaw. Red-gold fire climbed its blade in a narrow, controlled line.
“Close the channel.”
Sanguinar looked down the ranseur’s length. Light still burned around his hand. “He did not establish the yield.”
“You heard it.”
“I heard a claim from a man who still held a weapon.”
The point of the ranseur touched skin. “Close it.”
The Light went out.

Theron knelt beside Daric. The shoulder sat wrong beneath the armor, and Daric’s breath came in shallow pulls. A recovery knight cut the straps while Theron first sent a brief current around the break, stilling the bleeding and preventing the damaged joint from worsening when they moved it. Only after the armor was clear and the bone set did he call the slower restoration. Red-gold warmth entered tendon, muscle, and fractured bone by degrees. It repaired enough to preserve the arm, not enough to erase swelling, pain, or the weeks of recovery ahead.
Sanguinar watched without remorse. “In Outland, an enemy will not honor your limits.”
Falanaras stood over Daric with his sword still drawn. “Daric was not your enemy.”
“Then he should have been safer.”

Liadrin’s face had gone still. “An enemy’s dishonor does not release us from our own. You will leave at first transit tomorrow. You will take the three who completed the binding. The fourth remains here until he can face the truth inside the circle.”
“His Highness requested four.”
“His Highness will receive three.”
For the first time, Sanguinar’s satisfaction faltered. He bowed with open contempt and left the court.
Daric opened his eyes while the healers worked. Sweat shone across his brow.
“I withdraw my complaint about the weather,” he said.
Theron let out a breath that might have become laughter in a kinder hour. “Save your strength.”

Falanaras looked toward the archway where Sanguinar had disappeared. The order had been founded to make necessity answer discipline. Sanguinar had given his word, then broken the oath beneath it when obedience ceased to please him. He wanted victory freed from command, proportion, and the safety of anyone he did not consider an enemy. In his hands, strength ceased to serve and became permission.
M’uru’s pain still trembled beneath Falanaras’s breastbone.
Sanguinar crossed back into Outland at dawn.

The transit report reached Liadrin before midday. All four connections had endured the passage. Sanguinar’s first message from the far-side station contained no acknowledgment of Daric’s injury and no comment on M’uru’s pain. He reported combat readiness, stable access, and his intention to begin training candidates within Kael’thas’s army once Silvermoon supplied a method for additional bindings.

Astalor refused to send the apparatus plans. A living recipient still had to come before M’uru, and the designs exposed the controls by which Silvermoon subdued the naaru’s power and governed each bond. The method belonged to Silvermoon and the order it had created; he would not surrender its mastery to an Outland command beyond Silvermoon’s supervision. Liadrin supported the refusal. The matter went upward to Rommath and Lor’themar, where questions of authority became sealed correspondence.
Two days later, the Blood Knights prepared for another southern patrol.

Daric watched from a bench with his arm bound across his chest. The Light had repaired the worst damage, though the healers refused to restore full movement before the swelling eased. He criticized saddle straps while Theron inspected the shield file and Falanaras checked the strike weapons.
Lethira entered the courtyard carrying two message tubes and a look that promised inconvenience.
“The boundary wardens want a second recovery file,” she said. “Serenya’s scouts found fresh movement east of the Scar, and no one agrees whether it is Amani, Scourge, or both attempting cooperation.”
“That would show troubling initiative,” Theron said.
“I knew you would understand the strategic concern.” Lethira handed Falanaras the first tube. The second remained tucked beneath her arm. “This one is the route. The other is—”
Every ward-lamp in the courtyard dimmed at once.

The change lasted less than a heartbeat. Crimson light returned along the walls. Hawkstriders stamped and hissed in their lines. Falanaras felt no disturbance from M’uru’s presence within him, yet the arcane network beneath Silvermoon shuddered hard enough to tighten every trained muscle in his back.
A bell began ringing in the magisterial quarter. Three measured strokes, a pause, then three again.
Lethira’s expression changed. “Relay failure.”
Liadrin came through the opposite arch before Falanaras could answer. A magister followed at a run, his formal robes gathered in both hands. He carried a transit crystal whose center had gone black.
“Report,” Liadrin said.

“The Dark Portal has collapsed.” The magister struggled for breath. “The near-side garrison saw the field contract without warning. Travelers were assembling for passage. The surface went dark in front of them. All far-side contact ended in the same instant.”
No one in the courtyard moved.

Falanaras remembered the Portal as an impossible wall of green fire held inside ancient stone. He remembered the Outland engines pushing against it from beyond, the blood elf pylons steadying its edges, and the instructions to cross without pausing. Something powerful enough to end that field had acted between one breath and the next.
“Attack?” Theron asked.
“Unknown.”
“Failure of the stabilizing engines?” Falanaras asked.
“Unknown.” The magister looked down at the dead crystal. “The garrison is intact. The Portal itself is stone and darkness.”
Liadrin’s gaze found Daric’s bound arm. Then it moved to the empty place where Sanguinar had stood two days earlier.
“Can you sense anything of the four beyond it?” she asked.

The question was for Astalor, who had not yet arrived, but Falanaras reached instinctively toward his own connection. M’uru answered beneath the city, immediate and wounded. Beyond that presence lay nothing he could distinguish. He had never sensed the other knights as individuals through their shared source. The absence gave him no proof of death and no comfort of life.

Liadrin turned to the assembled order. “The southern patrol proceeds. Eversong does not become safer because the Portal has failed. Falanaras, Theron, take the original files. Add two recovery knights. Lethira, send your second report to Halduron and ride with them.”
Duty moved the courtyard again. Saddles tightened. Weapons returned to scabbards. The familiar work felt smaller than it had moments before, yet no less necessary.
As Falanaras mounted, the relay bell continued over Silvermoon.
The first explanations arrived before the Blood Knights returned from the boundary.

A stabilizing engine had failed in Hellfire Peninsula. Illidan had closed the route to punish Kael’thas. Human magi had sabotaged the Azeroth side. The prince had sealed the Portal himself while preparing a greater passage. A demon army had taken the far-side fortifications. Each account came from someone whose cousin had heard it from a clerk attached to a magister who possessed no answers.

By sunset, families crowded the Court of the Sun. They held letters that could no longer be sent and demanded names from officials who had received no casualty list. The magisters cordoned the annex. City guards kept the gathering from pressing against the wards. Every time the doors opened, the crowd surged toward them.

Falanaras stood with Liadrin beneath the annex portico after midnight. Theron had taken Daric home. Lethira carried Halduron’s sealed assessment to the regent. The remaining Blood Knights formed a line between frightened citizens and frightened clerks.
An elderly man pushed a letter toward Falanaras. “My daughter serves with the prince’s healers. The last dispatch said she was transferring to Netherstorm. You have been there.”
Falanaras looked at the careful seal, already softened where the man’s thumb had rubbed it. “Yes.”
“Then tell me whether she is safe.”

A lie would have cost little. Falanaras had seen officers spend them freely when fear threatened order. He had also carried Rynel’s final truth home from Deatholme and learned what duty became when facts were softened for comfort.

“I cannot tell you,” he said. “No message has crossed since the closure. If the Netherstorm positions remain as they were, she serves behind fortified lines. We do not know whether they remain as they were.”
The man’s hand lowered. He did not thank Falanaras. The letter remained clenched in his fist when a guard guided him away from the doors.
Liadrin watched him go. “You could have given him hope.”
“He already had hope. He asked for knowledge.”
“And we have none.”
The admission sounded angrier than any accusation. Liadrin had built herself around burdens that could be named, measured, and carried. Silence offered no weight to lift and no enemy to strike.

On the second day, Lor’themar issued a statement: the Portal garrison remained secure, Silvermoon’s magisters were investigating, and no evidence indicated the loss of Kael’thas or his forces. The careful wording steadied the markets for several hours. By evening, people were arguing over what the statement had refused to say.

Some insisted the prince would reopen the route as he had opened it before. Others claimed enemies in Silvermoon wanted contact broken. Veterans accused merchants of panic. Merchants accused the magisters of hoarding information. Outside the annex, someone began a prayer to the royal line and stopped halfway through, embarrassed by the old habit.
On the third night, Falanaras entered the receiving chamber with Liadrin, Astalor, and Rommath.

The circular platform stood empty. Its embedded crystals were dull. Before the closure, a faint pressure had always rested behind the relay wards, proof of the long chain reaching south to the Portal and beyond it. Falanaras had noticed the sensation only when it vanished.
Rommath finished the final diagnostic and lowered his hands. Arcane symbols faded around him.
“The Azeroth relays are functional,” he said. “The garrison can reach us by ordinary transport. The break is the gateway. Nothing crosses the threshold.”
“Can it be forced?” Liadrin asked.

“Perhaps. The first opening required Illidan’s power, Kael’thas’s magisters, and engines built in Outland. We possess one side of that effort.” Rommath’s expression remained severe. “Attempting the work blindly may destroy the standing frame or attract something prepared to answer.”

Astalor set the blackened transit crystal on the platform with unusual care. When he spoke, strain tightened his measured cadence. “Sanguinar’s channel has left no trace we can isolate from M’uru’s other currents. That tells us nothing. The world between us may conceal it. He may be drawing without interruption. He may be unable to draw. He may be dead.”
Liadrin’s eyes flashed gold beneath the green. “You take comfort in precision.”

“There is no comfort in this.” Astalor’s voice sharpened, and the break from his habitual restraint made the words carry. “Four bonds fashioned for our order now lie beyond Silvermoon’s reach. We cannot determine whether they endure, whether they have failed, or what is being done through them. I will not make that danger sound smaller.”

Falanaras stood at the platform’s edge. Three days earlier, Sanguinar had crossed with stolen Light inside him and Kael’thas’s certainty before him. Falanaras had been relieved to see him go. The memory now carried shame, though he could not decide what better wish he should have made.
“Contact had been stable,” he said. “The far side reported no attack. Sanguinar crossed safely. Supply requests came through the previous cycle.”
Rommath looked at him. “Yes.”
“Then either they did not know this was coming, or they did not warn us.”
The chamber held the words without answering them.

Falanaras had spent years believing distance explained the prince’s silence. Kael’thas fought in another world. Messages required ships, hidden roads, guarded relays, and powers beyond ordinary reach. Every delay had possessed a reason. Every order that arrived renewed the promise connecting Silvermoon’s suffering to his purpose.
Now the road had vanished while certainty was still traveling upon it.

Beneath the city, M’uru remained in chains. Along the southern boundary, the Blood Knights kept watch. Outland held Kael’thas, Sanguinar, and thousands of sin’dorei beyond any answer Silvermoon could compel.
The relay platform stayed dark.
